correctness.rationale: Conditioning on the training mean \(\widehat\mu\), the evaluation log e-value is \((n-m)(\widehat\mu\bar Y_0-\widehat\mu^2/2)\). Under \(N(\mu,1)\), independence of the split gives \(\mathbb E\widehat\mu=\mu\), \(\mathbb E\widehat\mu^2=\mu^2+1/m\), hence the exact e-power formula. Direct subtraction gives the forward difference and therefore complete integer unimodality/tie characterization. The positivity threshold, local scaling, and fixed-signal expansion follow from that threshold relation. Independently, 3471 \((n,\mu)\) cases including every adjacent-tie value for \(2\le n<80\) were optimized over all integer splits and matched the threshold characterization exactly.

value.rationale: E-power is a standard growth-rate criterion for e-values, and sample allocation is a central design choice in universal inference. The exact law reveals a qualitatively different optimum from fixed-fraction heuristics: under fixed signal the training fraction vanishes at rate \(n^{-1/2}\), while under local alternatives it has a nontrivial phase boundary at \(|h|=1\). That makes the calculation a motivated benchmark rather than a routine parameter substitution.
residual_risks: The oracle criterion alone does not establish that using this split maximizes ordinary rejection probability.

final_claim: For the scalar known-variance Gaussian split universal likelihood ratio with \(n\ge2\), training size \(m\), evaluation size \(n-m\), and true mean \(\mu\), the e-power is \[G_n(m;\mu)=\frac{n-m}{2}\left(\mu^2-\frac1m\right).\] Its forward difference is \(\frac12\{n/[m(m+1)]-\mu^2\}\), giving the exact integer oracle split, adjacent-tie boundaries, positivity threshold \(\mu^2>1/(n-1)\), local-alternative limit \(m_n/n\to\min\{1,1/|h|\}\) for \(\mu=h/\sqrt n\) with limiting maximum \((|h|-1)_+^2/2\), and fixed-signal law \(m_n=\sqrt n/|\mu|+O(1)\) with maximum e-power \(n\mu^2/2-\sqrt n|\mu|+O(1)\).
limitations: Scalar Gaussian location with known unit variance and a single fixed train/evaluation split.
The oracle split depends on the true alternative mean and is a benchmark, not a directly implementable data-adaptive procedure.
No claim is made for repeated subsampling, unknown variance, composite nulls, or higher-dimensional means.
